title: Cap. VI Arg. 12: second — separation follows Peter's act, not God's segregating decree
pass_a_gloss: Secondly, we acknowledge according to the tenor of the aforesaid decree that Peter is to be separated unto eternal life after he shall have persevered in faith: but this separation follows from the consequent and contingent act of Peter himself, it does not arise from a segregative decree of God himself. For by his own act he was segregated unto salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered, but by the aforesaid decree he was not singularly segregated, whether unto faith or unto salvation. Let this be illustrated by a like case. If a King should enact such a decree, Whosoever shall have climbed the walls of the besieged city shall become a knight; whosoever shall have turned his back shall be punished with death, they are singular persons who scale the walls, singular persons who flee: and yet by such a decree the King is not said to have elected certain singular persons unto knightly dignity, and to have passed by others; but to have conferred it upon singular persons; and to have destined that dignity equally to all, either to be obtained if they behave well, or to be lost if otherwise. Such in all points is that Arminian election; and therefore it does not have included a true and real separation of singular persons.
pass_b_english: Second: we grant that by that decree's tenor Peter is to be set apart to eternal life once he has persevered in faith — but that separation follows from Peter's own consequent contingent act, not from a segregating decree of God. By his act he was set apart to salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered; by the decree itself he was not singularly segregated unto faith or salvation. Like case: if a king enacts Whoever scales the besieged city's walls shall be knighted; whoever turns his back shall die — those who climb and those who flee are singular persons; yet the king is not said to have elected certain singulars to knighthood and passed others by, but to have conferred it on singulars and destined that dignity equally to all — to be won if they behave well, lost if not. Arminian election is of that kind throughout, and so includes no true real separation of singular persons.
source_text: Secundo, agnoscimus juxta tenorem praedicti decreti Petrum ad vitam aeternam separandum, postquam in fide perseveraverit: sed haec separatio consequitur ex consequente et contingente actu ipsius Petri, non oritur ex segregativo decreto ipsius Dei. Suo enim actu fuit segregatus ad salutem postquam praevisus est credidisse et perseverasse, sed praedicto decreto non fuit singulariter segregatus, sive ad fidem sive ad salutem. Simili hoc illustretur. Si Rex tale decretum sanciat, Quisquis muros oppugnatae urbis ascenderit, eques fiet; quisquis terga verterit, capite plectetur, singulares personae sunt qui muros scandunt, singulares personae qui fugiunt: neque tamen tali decreto dicitur Rex elegisse singulares quasdam personas ad equestrem dignitatem, alias autem praeteriisse; sed contulisse in singulares personas; destinasse autem illam dignitatem ex aequo omnibus, sive obtinendam, si bene se gesserint, sive amittendam, si secus. Talis per omnia est illa electio Arminiana; ac proinde non habet inclusam veram et realem separationem singularium personarum.
